Complete Positivity for Mixed Unitary Categories
Robin Cockett, Priyaa Varshinee Srinivasan

Abstract
Coecke and Heunen described completely positive maps in dagger monoidal categories and the CP -infinity construction on these categories in order to construct a category of arbitrary dimensional quantum processes. This article generalizes the 𝖢𝖯 \mathsf{CP} -infinity construction of dagger monoidal categories to mixed unitary categories. Mixed unitary categories, on the one hand, generalize the (compact) dagger monoidal categories, and on the other hand, accommodate arbitrary dimensional quantum processes, both without sacrificing the notion of dual objects. This means that the 𝖢𝖯 \mathsf{CP} -infinity construction for mixed unitary categories provides a suitable semantics for higher-order quantum programming languages which employ arbitrary dimensional structures. The existing results for the 𝖢𝖯 \mathsf{CP} -infinity construction are shown to generalize to the new setting. In particular, the notion of environment structures generalizes to mixed unitary categories and it is shown that the 𝖢𝖯 \mathsf{CP} -infinity construction for mixed unitary categories is characterized by this generalized environment structure.



1
Introduction

Categorical quantum mechanics (CQM) uses Hilbert spaces as the
de facto
model
for quantum systems. The category of finite
dimensional Hilbert spaces and linear maps, which are dagger compact closed, are
used as a diagrammatic framework to describe and reason about quantum processes. A well-known
limitation of such compact closed categories is that they model finite dimensional
Hilbert spaces, but they cannot model infinite dimensional spaces
[
16
]
.
Due to this restriction, practical applications of CQM, so far, have been
focused on the areas such as quantum computing and quantum information theory
which are off-shoots of finite dimensional quantum mechanics.

The success of CQM in the study of finite dimensional processes has inspired researchers to extend CQM frameworks to include infinite dimensional processes
[
13
,
15
,
3
,
22
,
17
]
.
The most common approach has been to work within a dagger monoidal setting since the category of arbitrary dimensional Hilbert spaces is dagger monoidal (but not compact closed).
However, such an approach is not quite satisfactory since, in these categories, the objects need not have duals (a feature which allows wires to be “bent” in the graphical calculus).

In
[
10
]
, the authors and Comfort addressed this dimensionality issue by generalizing the framework of dagger monoidal categories to mixed unitary categories (MUCs) which are based on linearly distributive categories and
*
-autonomous categories, see Section
2
for more details. In order to define MUCs, one starts by defining dagger functor for linearly distributive categories. The dagger functor abstracts the notion of unitary evolution of quantum systems by capturing the notion of adjoints. The dagger functor is identity-on-objects for monoidal categories, which forces the objects in a dagger monoidal category to be self-adjoint. However, this is not the case in linearly distributive categories. Indeed, describing the dagger functor for LDCs leads one to a description of unitary isomorphisms for unitary (or self-adjoint) objects. This also leads one to the isomix version of dagger LDCs (a setting in which truth and false are isomorphic). By collecting the unitary objects of a dagger isomix category, one gets a unitary category, which is equivalent to a dagger monoidal category but sitting inside the larger setting of dagger isomix categories: this is the setting of a mixed unitary category. See Figure
1
schematic of the mixed unitary category:

A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.43474pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\varphi_{A}$}}_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}A^{\dagger}
Unitary
category

\dagger

Figure 1:
Schematic of mixed unitary categories

Mixed unitary categories allow the presence dual objects without the restriction of finite dimensionality. While every dagger monoidal category is certainly a mixed unitary category the reverse is not the case. Examples of MUCs include Chu spaces
[
4
]
and finiteness spaces
[
14
]
which have been used to model infinite dimensional systems in physics and in computer science
[
1
,
2
,
18
,
21
,
27
]
.
The aim of this article is to describe quantum processes in the general setting of mixed unitary categories.

In a dagger compact closed category, a (finite dimensional) quantum process is given by a map of the shape shown in Figure
2
-(a) below. Such a map is a called a completely positive map because it is an abstract representation of the Kraus decomposition of completely positive linear maps between
\mathbb{C}^{\star}
algebras
[
7
]
. In order to
describe arbitrary dimensional quantum processes diagrammatically, Coecke and Heunen dropped the requirement of

compactness
and moved to the setting of dagger symmetric monoidal categories (
\dagger
-SMCs). Since, wires cannot be “bent” in general in a dagger symmetric monoidal category, they straightened the environment wire
E
in diagram (a) below to obtaining completely positive maps with a hole as shown in Figure
2
-(b). In this manner Coecke and Heunen provided the
{\sf CP}
-infinity construction which would turn any
\dagger
-SMC into one with completely positive maps, and, furthermore, they axiomatized the construction using environment structures.

(a)

Figure 2:
(a) A completely positive map in a dagger compact closed category; (b) A completely positive map in a dagger monoidal category

This article describes completely positive maps for MUCs, and generalizes the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction from dagger monoidal categories to MUCs, developing an axiomatic description of this construction using generalized environment structures. This generalization is not straight forward because unlike in dagger monoidal and dagger-compact closed categories, objects are not in general self-adjoint in a MUC, that is, for an arbitrary object
A
in the category,
A\neq A^{\dagger}
. This means a map
g
cannot be composed with its dagger as shown in Figure
2
-(b) along the environment wire
E
(because,
E
is not necessarily equal to
E^{\dagger}
). This problem can be resolved by requiring the object
E
to be
unitary
(meaning
E\simeq E^{\dagger}
, see Section
2.2
). This allows a formulation of completely positive maps in MUCs, see Section
5.1
for details. The
CP
-infinity construction for MUCs is discussed in Section
5.2
. The
CP
-infinity construction on a MUC does not, in general, result in a MUC unless every object has a dual. The structures which are inherited by the construction are discussed in Section
5.3
. The proofs in this article extensively use the graphical calculus for MUCs developed in Section
4
.

The more sophisticated type system of MUCs becomes important when axiomatizing the
CP
-infinity construction in terms of the environment structures. A dagger monoidal category is said to have an environment structure when every object in the category is equipped with a discarding map
d:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}I
(loosely, information held by an object can be discarded freely): this must behave coherently with the dagger monoidal structure. An environment structure for a MUC, on the other hand demands such discarding maps only for the unitary objects. The definition of an environment structure for MUCs and how they are used to axiomatize the
CP
-infinity construction is discussed in Section
6
and uses the notion of dagger linear functors developed in Section
3
. Notably, when a MUC is a dagger monoidal category, one faithfully recovers Coecke and Heunen’s
CP
-infinity construction from the
CP
-infinity construction of MUCs.

A motivation for describing completely positive maps in MUCs is that it may provide a suitable semantics for higher-order quantum programming languages. Selinger and Valiron
[
26
]
described a model of a higher-order linear quantum programming language based on the CPM (completely positive maps) construction on the category of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces and linear maps. However, the existing models
[
24
,
8
,
9
,
20
,
26
]
fall short in satisfactorily handling the preservation of the total probability of higher order computations due to the infinite sums involved. Moreover, infinite datatypes and recursion is handled by augmenting the CPM category with additional properties like infinite biproducts
[
20
]
. Having a description of completely positive maps in MUCs enables an investigation of richer models of higher-order quantum computation without some of the drawback listed above.

Note:
This article assumes some familiarity with linearly distributive categories (LDCs), mix categories, linear adjoints, linearly distributive functors and linear transformations
[
11
]
,
*
-autonomous categories, and dagger compact closed categories
[
25
]
. We recall the definition of these structures in Appendix
A
. A review of these structures is also available in
[
10
, Sec. 2]
.

2
Preliminaries: Mixed unitary categories

Mixed unitary categories draw inspiration from the proof theory of multiplicative linear logic, with categorical semantics in linearly distributive categories. In
[
10
,
27
]
it is shown how to coherently add a dagger (
\dagger
) to the doctrine of linearly distributive categories (and
*
-autonomous categories) to obtain the proof theory of
\dagger
-linear logic.

Linearly distributive categories are categories with two monoidal structures called the tensor,
\otimes
, and the par
\oplus
linked by natural transformations called linear distributors:

\partial^{L}:A\otimes(B\oplus C)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\otimes B)\oplus C~~~~~~~~\partial^{R}:(A\oplus B)\otimes C\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus(B\otimes C)

The distributor is referred to as linear because, unlike in the usual distribution of product over sums,
A\times(B+C)\simeq(A\times B)+(A\times C)
, in the linear distribution, type
A
is not duplicated.

In order to model quantum processes it is necessary, firstly, to specialize to the “mix” case of linear logic in where there is a coherent transformation from the tensor to the par of two objects
{\sf mx}:A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus B
(and an isomorphism
{\sf m}:\top\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\bot
from the tensor unit to the par unit).

In order to model quantum structures one needs a notion of “unitary structure”. This is determined by objects
U
which are in the core (that is for which
{\sf mx}:U\otimes X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U\oplus X
is an isomorphism) and which are equipped with a (coherent) isomorphism
\varphi:U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U^{\dagger}
. The subcategory of unitary objects form a
\dagger
-monoidal category which sits inside a larger category of quantum processes. Intuitively one may think of the unitary objects as being the finite dimensional objects of the setting and thus potentially forming a standard model of CQM. From this perspective, a mixed unitary category consists of a standard model of CQM sitting in a larger category which models the proof theory of
\dagger
-linear logic and includes infinite dimensional processes.

2.1
Dagger linearly distributive categories

Conventionally, in categorical quantum mechanics a dagger is defined as a contravariant
endofunctor which is stationary on objects (
A^{\dagger}=A
) and an involution (
f^{\dagger\dagger}=f
). However,
in an LDC where there are two tensor products interacting by linear distribution (
\partial^{L}:A\otimes(B\oplus C)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\otimes B)\oplus C
), and the dagger must minimally flip the tensor products to
maintain the directionality of the distributor maps. This because, if the dagger were stationary on objects it would provide a map
\partial^{\dagger}:(A\otimes B)\oplus C\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\otimes(B\oplus C)
: this is not a valid map an LDC. Hence, unlike for dagger monoidal categories, a dagger for an LDC cannot be stationary on objects. However, it is still possible for it to be an involution.

.

A dagger linearly distributive category is an LDC with a functor

\displaystyle A\xrightarrow{\iota}(A^{\dagger})^{\dagger}

such that certain coherence conditions hold

.

2.2
Unitary isomorphisms in dagger LDCs

The notion of unitary maps is central to both quantum information theory as well as quantum mechanics since the evolution of a closed quantum system is described by such maps. Categorically, within a
\dagger
-category, a unitary map is an isomorphism
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
such that
f^{-1}=f^{\dagger}
. This definiton of unitary isomorphism cannot be used directly within the framework of
\dagger
-LDCs since the types of
f^{-1}:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A
and
f^{\dagger}:B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\dagger}
are different. It is therefore
apparent that one can only ask to have unitary isomorphisms between certain objects, which we call “unitary objects”:

Definition 2.6
.

A
unitary category
is a
\dagger
-isomix category
\mathbb{U}
in which every object is unitary.

We can now define what it means for a isomorphism to be unitary:

Definition 2.7
.

Suppose
A
and
B
are unitary objects. An isomorphism
A\xrightarrow{f}B
is said to be a
unitary isomorphism
if the following diagram commutes:

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\scriptstyle{f}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{B}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f^{\dagger}}

Observe that
\varphi
is “twisted” natural for all unitary isomorphisms, thus, unitary isomorphisms compose and contain the identity maps. In a category in which the unitary structure maps are identity morphisms, one recovers the usual notion of unitary isomorphisms.

Often we shall want the unitary objects to have linear adjoints (or duals) but we shall need the analogue of dagger duals from categorical quantum mechanics
[
25
, Defn. 2.6]
:

Definition 2.8
.

A
unitary linear duality

(\eta,\varepsilon):A\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}B
between unitary objects
A
and
B
is a linear duality satisfying in addition:

\textstyle{{\bf[Udual.]}}

\textstyle{\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(a)}
\scriptstyle{\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\top}}
\textstyle{A\oplus B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}\oplus\varphi_{B}}
\textstyle{\bot^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varepsilon^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\oplus B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{c_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{(B\otimes A)^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1}}
\textstyle{B^{\dagger}\oplus A^{\dagger}}

\textstyle{A\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(b)}
\scriptstyle{\varphi_{A}\otimes\varphi_{B}}
\scriptstyle{c_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{A^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{B\otimes A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varepsilon}
\textstyle{(A\oplus B)^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\eta^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\lambda_{\bot}}
\textstyle{\top^{\dagger}}

In a
\dagger
-monoidal monoidal category, the above described unitary duality precisely coincides with the notion of dagger duals.

Lemma 2.9
.

Suppose
(\eta_{1},\varepsilon_{1}):V_{1}\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}U_{1}
and
(\eta_{2},\varepsilon_{2}):V_{2}\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}U_{2}
. Then,
(V_{1}\otimes V_{2})\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}(U_{1}\oplus U_{2})
.

2.3
Mixed unitary categories

With the definition of unitary objects in place, one could ask for a
\dagger
-isomix category in which all the objects are unitary; or a
\dagger
-isomix category with a full sub
\dagger
-isomix category of unitary objects. The former notion is formalized by so called unitary categories, generalising
\dagger
-monoidal categories; the latter is formalized by so called mixed unitary categories.

A unitary category is a compact LDC by defintion. A
\dagger
-monoidal category is a strict unitary category in which the unitary structure map and the mix map are identity morphisms. Similarily, a
\dagger
-compact closed category is a strict unitary category in which all objects have unitary duals.

A mixed unitary category (MUC) can be schematically represented as follows. Informally, a MUC is a unitary category that ‘lives’ within the core of a dagger-isomix category. Recall that for any object
U
within the core and for any other object A,
U\otimes A\simeq U\otimes B
, and
U\otimes A\simeq U\otimes B
. See Figure
1
for a schematic representation of mixed unitary categories.

The formal definition of MUCs is given below:

Definition 2.10
.

A
mixed unitary category
(MUC) is a
\dagger
-isomix category,
\mathbb{C}
, equipped with a strong
\dagger
-isomix functor

M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
from a unitary category
\mathbb{U}
to
\mathbb{C}
such that there exists the following natural transformations:

\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}:M(U)\oplus X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M(U)\otimes X\text{ with }\mathsf{mx}~\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}=1\text{ and }\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}~\mathsf{mx}=1

\mathsf{mx}^{\prime\prime}:X\oplus M(U)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}X\otimes M(U)\text{ with }\mathsf{mx}~\mathsf{mx}^{\prime\prime}=1\text{ and }\mathsf{mx}^{\prime\prime}~\mathsf{mx}=1

A mixed unitary category,
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
is
symmetric
if the functor
M
, the
unitary category
\mathbb{U}
, and the
\dagger
-isomix category
\mathbb{C}
are symmetric. If
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
is an MUC where
\mathbb{C}
is a
*
-autonomous category, then
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
is said to be a
*
-MUC
. If moreover every object in
\mathbb{U}
has unitary duals,
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
is said to be a
*
-mixed unitary category with duals
(
*
-MUdC).

In the definition of a MUC, the requirement of a transformation
\mathsf{mx}^{\prime}
which is inverse to
\mathsf{mx}
ensures that the functor

M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
factors through
\mathsf{Core}(\mathbb{C})
.

All dagger monoidal categories together with the identity functor are mixed unitary categories. The inclusion of a full subcategory of unitary objects of a
\dagger
-isomix category with unitary structure is a MUC.

A functor between two MUCs
(\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.37639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M$}}}\mathbb{C})
and
(\mathbb{V}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to19.08472pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$N$}}}\mathbb{Y})
is a square commuting upto
\dagger
-linear natural isomorphism
\gamma
:

\textstyle{\mathbb{U}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\gamma}
\scriptstyle{M}
\textstyle{\mathbb{X}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F}
\textstyle{\mathbb{V}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{N}
\textstyle{\mathbb{Y}}

F
and
F^{\prime}
are
\dagger
-isomix functors and
F^{\prime}
preserves unitary structure. See Section
3
for the definition of a
\dagger
-linear natural isomorphism and conditions for preservation of unitary structure.

2.4
Examples of MUCs

An important source of examples of MUCs is given by considering an LDC and the inclusion functor of its core. Thus, the category of finite dimensional framed vector spaces and linear maps, finiteness modules, and the category of Chu spaces of complex vector spaces over
\mathbb{X}
give MUCs in this manner
[
10
]
. Any
\dagger
-monoidal category is also a MUC with
M=id
and the unitary structure given by identity maps. In fact, every unitary category is equivalent to a
\dagger
-monoidal category: in a unitary category, however, the
\dagger
is not assumed to be stationary on objects but merely isomorphic via the unitary structure map.

In this article, we shall exemplify our constructions on the following two examples of MUCs:

Example 2.11
.

(1)

\mathbb{R}^{*}\subset\mathbb{C}
: consider the discrete monoidal category,
\mathbb{C}
, of complex numbers defined as follows:

Objects:

a+ib\in\mathbb{C}

Maps:

Identity maps only
c=c

Tensor:

multiplication is given by
(a+ib)\otimes(x+iy):=(ax-by)+i(ay+bx)
with the unit 1

Dagger:

(a+ib)^{\dagger}:=a-ib

\mathbb{C}
is a compact LDC (that is
\otimes\simeq\oplus
) with a non-stationary dagger functor.

The subcategory
\mathbb{R}^{*}
of non-zero real numbers is a unitary category with the unitary structure map given by identity maps. Thus,
\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}
is a mixed unitary category.

(2)

\mathsf{Mat}_{\mathbb{C}}\subset\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
: The second example uses finiteness spaces
[
14
]
. A
finiteness space
,
(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, consists of a set
X
and subsets
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subseteq P(X)
such that
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A}^{\perp}
, in the sense that

\mathcal{B}=\{b|b\in P(X)\text{ with for all }a\in A,|a\cap b|<\infty\},

and
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}^{\perp}
.

A
finiteness relation
,
(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.06007pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$R$}}}(Y,\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
is relation
X\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.06007pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$R$}}}Y
such that

\forall A\in\mathcal{A}.AR\in\mathcal{A}^{\prime}~~\mbox{and}~~\forall B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime}.RB^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}

Finiteness spaces with finiteness relation form a
*
-autonomous category
[
14
]
. One can define a category of finiteness matrices,
\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
as follows:

Objects:

Finiteness spaces
(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})

Maps:

(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.37639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M$}}}(Y,\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
is a matrix
X\times Y\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.37639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M$}}}\mathbb{C}
such that

supp(M):=\{(x,y)|x\in X,y\in Y\text{ and }M(x,y)\neq 0\}

is a finiteness relation from
(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
to
(Y,\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
.

Dagger:

(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})^{\dagger}:=(X,\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
and
M^{\dagger}
is the complex conjugate of
M
.

The finiteness typing of these matrices ensures that on matrix composition the sums are always finite.
{\sf Mat}_{\mathbb{C}}
, the category of finite matrices over complex numbers is a full subcategory of
\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
which is determined by the objects,
(X,P(X),P(X))
, where
X
is a finite set.
{\sf Mat}_{\mathbb{C}}
is a unitary category (with unitary structure given by identity maps), and is a well-known
\dagger
-compact closed category. The inclusion
{\sf Mat}_{\mathbb{C}}\subset\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
is a mixed unitary category.

3
Dagger linear functors

(For definition of linear functors, see Appendix
B
.)

Clearly the functors and transformations between
\dagger
-LDCs must “preserve” the dagger in some sense. Precisely we have:

Definition 3.1
.

F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a
\dagger
-linear functor
between
\dagger
-LDCs when it is a linear functor equipped with a linear natural isomorphism

\rho^{F}=(\rho_{\otimes}^{F}:F_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A)^{\dagger},\rho_{\oplus}^{F}:F_{\otimes}(A)^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger}))
called the
preservator
,
such that the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F_{\otimes}(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-LF.1]
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\oplus})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F_{\oplus}(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-LF.2]
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\otimes})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

Observe that when
F
is a mix functor between
\dagger
-isomix categories, then
F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}
and the preservators become pairwise inverses:
\rho^{F}_{\otimes}=(\rho^{F}_{\oplus})^{-1}
.
This means the squares
[
\dagger
-LF.1]
and
[
\dagger
-LF.2]
coincide to give a single condition for the tensor preservator:

\textstyle{F(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\iota}
\scriptstyle{F(\iota)}
[
\dagger
-isomix]
\textstyle{F(X)^{\dagger\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\rho^{F}_{\otimes})^{\dagger}}
\textstyle{F(X^{\dagger\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\otimes}}
\textstyle{F(X^{\dagger})^{\dagger}}

For linear natural transformations
\beta:F\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}G
between
\dagger
-linear functors we demand that
\beta_{\otimes}
and
\beta_{\oplus}

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A^{\dagger})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{(F_{\oplus}(X))^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{(G_{\otimes}(X))^{\dagger}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\scriptstyle{\rho^{F}_{\oplus}}

\scriptstyle{\beta_{\oplus}}
\textstyle{F_{\oplus}(A^{\dagger})}

We call these
\dagger
-linear natural transformations
. Notice that this means that
\beta_{\otimes}
is completely determined by
\beta_{\oplus}
in the following sense:

\textstyle{F_{\otimes}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\scriptstyle{\beta_{\otimes}}

Because the vertical maps are isomorphisms, this diagram can be used to express
\beta_{\otimes}
in terms of
\beta_{\oplus}
. Similarly
\beta_{\oplus}
can be expressed in terms
of
\beta_{\otimes}
. Thus, it is possible to express the coherences in terms of just one of these transformations.

Our next step is to generalize the
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}
-construction on dagger monoidal categories to the mixed unitary categories. We first introduce a circuit calculus for mixed unitary categories which is an extension of proof nets of linearly distributive categories and is similar to the pictures used in classical categorical quantum mechanics.

4
String Calculus for Mixed Unitary Categories

To facilitate reasoning within MUCs, it is useful to employ a circuit calculus built on the circuit calculus for LDCs introduced in
[
6
]
. The extended circuit calculus for mixed unitary categories includes dagger boxes, components for unitary structure maps, and inverse mixor morphisms.

5
Quantum channels for mixed unitary categories

In quantum mechanics, the representation of a physical state can be either
pure

or
mixed
. A representation is mixed when it is a statistical ensemble of
possible states of the system. If the representation is pure, then one knows the exact
quantum state of the system. While a pure state is represented as a vector in a
Hilbert Space, a mixed state is represented as a positive self-adjoint operator on the
Hilbert Space. The mixed state formalism of quantum mechanics is very useful in
practice since in an experimental setting our knowledge about the state of
a quantum system is often limited.

In the mixed state formalism, a quantum process is a completely positive map (sending
positive self-adjoint operators to positive self-adjoint operators) which preserves
trace.

The following theorem by Choi characterizes the form of completely positive maps:

Theorem 5.1
.

[
7
, Theorem 1]
Let
H
and
K
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces.
A linear map
\varphi:\mathcal{L}(H)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathcal{L}(K)
is completely
positive if and only if there exists a collection of linear maps,
\{M_{i}|M_{i}\in\mathcal{L}(H,K)

such that for all
A\in\mathcal{L}(H)
,

\varphi(A)=\sum_{i}M_{i}^{\dagger}AM_{i}

where
M_{i}^{\dagger}
is a adjoint of
M_{i}
.

The equation in the above theorem is referred to as the
Kraus decomposition
of
\varphi
, and the
collection of maps,
\{M_{i}|M_{i}\in\mathcal{L}(H,K)
, are referred to as the
Kraus operators
.

In this section, we discuss completely positive maps in the MUC setting. We begin by describing Kraus maps in MUCs based on the formulation of Kraus maps for dagger monoidal categories
[
13
]
.

5.1
Kraus maps

Definition 5.2
.

A
Kraus map

(f,U):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
in a mixed unitary category,
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
, is a map
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M(U)\oplus B\in\mathbb{C}
for some
U\in\mathbb{U}
.
U
is called the ancillary system of
f
.

Note that, while a Kraus map
(f,U)
can be between arbitrary types, the ancillary system,
U
, is always a unitary object.

A Kraus map may be connected to its dagger along its ancillary system giving rise to a combinator which acts on “test maps”. Two Kraus maps are equivalent when their effects on test maps are indistinguishable.

Definition 5.3
.

Given a MUC,
\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.37639pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M$}}}\mathbb{C}
, two Kraus maps
(f,U),(g,V):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
are
equivalent
,
(f,U)\sim(g,V)
, if for all
test maps

h:B\otimes C\rightarrow M(W)
, where
C\in C
and
W\in\mathbb{U}
, the following equality holds:

Note that the
\mathsf{mx}^{-1}
map can be slid up and down along the wires of the ancillary objects
M(U)
and
M(V)
by naturality of the
\mathsf{mx}
map. The diagram includes covariant functor boxes for
M
and contravariant functor boxes for the dagger. The lefthand diagram is given equationally as follows:

A\otimes C\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to30.56218pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f\otimes 1$}}}(X\oplus B)\otimes C\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.63472pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\delta$}}}X\oplus(B\otimes C)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to30.55984pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$1\oplus h$}}}M(U)\oplus M(W)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to25.37222pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\mathsf{mx}^{-1}$}}}M(U)\otimes M(W)

\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to70.49136pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$M(\varphi_{U})\otimes M(\varphi_{V})$}}}M(U^{\dagger})\otimes M(V^{\dagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to30.18994pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\rho\otimes\rho$}}}M(U)^{\dagger}\otimes M(W)^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to48.81406pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$1\otimes(h^{\dagger}\lambda_{\oplus}^{-1})$}}}M(U)^{\dagger}\otimes(B^{\dagger}\oplus C^{\dagger})

\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to15.63472pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\delta$}}}(M(U)^{\dagger}\otimes B^{\dagger})\oplus C^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to33.1113pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\otimes}\oplus 1$}}}(M(U)\oplus B)^{\dagger}\oplus C^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to31.41898pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f^{\dagger}\oplus 1$}}}A^{\dagger}\oplus C^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to21.05417pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\lambda_{\oplus}$}}}(A\otimes C)^{\dagger}

The natural isomorphism
\rho:M(U^{\dagger})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M(U)^{\dagger}
is the preservator of the
\dagger
-isomix functor,
M
, which ensures coherence with the
\dagger
from
\mathbb{U}
to
\mathbb{C}
.

An equivalence class of Kraus morphisms is a
quantum channel
. If
(f,U):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
and
(g,V):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
are Kraus maps for which
U
and
V
are unitarily isomorphic, they are necessarily equivalent with respect to this relation:

Lemma 5.4
.

Let
(f,U),(g,V):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
be Kraus morphisms. If
~U\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to17.19875pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\alpha$}}}V
is a unitary isomorphism and
f(\alpha\oplus 1)=g
, then
(f,U)\sim(g,V)
.

-MUC, the equivalence relation on Kraus maps is given equationally as follows:

.

(f,U)
and
(g,V)

Let us now examine Kraus maps in our running examples:

Example 5.6
.

(1)

In the MUC,
\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}
, let
c,c^{\prime}
be any two complex numbers. Kraus maps in
\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}
are
(=,r):c\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}c^{\prime}
such that
c=rc^{\prime}.
If
c^{\prime}\neq 0
, then there is at most one Kraus map
(=,r):c\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}c^{\prime}
. If
c^{\prime}=0
, then
c=0
and for all
r^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}
,
(=,r)\sim(=,r^{\prime}):c\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}c^{\prime}
. Thus, in the complex plane, there are only Kraus maps between those complex numbers that can be connected by a line that extends through the origin making it a
2
-dimensional projective space.

\mathbb{R}
\iota

(2)

In
\mathsf{Mat}_{\mathbb{C}}\subset\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
, every Kraus map
(M,\mathbb{C}^{n}):(X,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\perp})\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(Y,\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}^{\perp})
is given by the sum of
pure completely positive maps
i.e.,Kraus maps with
\mathbb{C}
as ancillary object:

M
(X,\mathcal{A})
M^{\dagger}
(X,\mathcal{A}^{\perp})
N
N^{\dagger}
(Y,\mathcal{B})
\mathbb{C}^{m}
(Y,\mathcal{B}^{\perp})

Choi’s theorem
states that every completely positive map can be written as a sum of pure completely positive maps. Analogously, every Kraus map in the category
\mathsf{FMat}_{\mathbb{C}}
can be written as a sum of pure maps as above. Given a Kraus map
(M,\mathbb{C}^{m})
, here is the argument:

\displaystyle(M\otimes 1)(1\otimes NN^{\dagger})(M^{\dagger}\oplus 1)

\displaystyle=(M\otimes 1)\left(\left(\sum_{i}\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{0.0}{$\prod$}}$}}_{i}\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{0.0}{$\prod$}}_{i}\right)\otimes NN^{\dagger}\right)(M^{\dagger}\oplus 1)

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\left((M(\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{180.0}{$\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{0.0}{$\prod$}}$}}_{i}\otimes 1)\otimes 1)(1\otimes hh^{\dagger})(((\mathbin{\rotatebox[origin]{0.0}{$\prod$}}_{i}\oplus 1)M^{\dagger})\oplus 1)\right)

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(M_{i}\otimes 1)(1\otimes NN^{\dagger})(M_{i}^{\dagger}\oplus 1)

5.2
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction for MUCs

The CPM construction
[
25
]
on dagger compact closed categories applied to the concrete category of finite dimensional Hilbert Spaces and linear maps produces a category of mixed states and quantum processes. Coecke and Heunen
[
13
]
generalized the CPM construction to
{\dagger}
-symmetric monoidal categories, and thus, to infinite dimensions. They call the generalized construction the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction. In this section, we generalize the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction to MUCs: thus, our construction coincides with the original
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction when the MUC is a
\dagger
-monoidal category.

The
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction for mixed unitary categories is as follows:

Definition 5.7
.

Given a mixed unitary category,
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
, define
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
to have:

Objects:

Same as
\mathbb{C}

Maps:

Equivalence classes of Kraus morphisms from X. That is,
[(f,U)]:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
is
(f,U):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathbb{X}\ /\sim\in M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
,

Composition:

Given maps
[(f,U)]:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B
and
[(g,V)]:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}C
in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
, composition is defined as

[(f,U)][(g,V)]:=A\xrightarrow{f}U\oplus B\xrightarrow{1\oplus g}U\oplus(V\oplus C)\xrightarrow{a_{\oplus}}(U\oplus V)\oplus C\in\mathbb{C}

Graphically, this is represented by the following map in
\mathbb{C}
:

f
g
M

Identity:

1_{A}
is defined as
[A\xrightarrow{(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}}\bot\oplus A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to45.6217pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$(n_{\bot}^{M})^{-1}\oplus 1$}}}M(\bot)\oplus A]\in\mathbb{X}

To prove that
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})

.

\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
is a category.

5.3
Structures inherited by the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction

While the
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}
construction described in the previous section produces a category of equivalence classes of Kraus morphisms in a MUC, it is desirable to know if the resulting category inherits dagger and LDC structures from the base category.

The following table summarizes the structures inherited by
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
from
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
for different variants of MUCs:

M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}

\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}
(
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
)

mixed unitary category

isomix category

*
-mixed unitary category with unitary duals

*
-mixed unitary category with unitary duals

\dagger
-symmetric monoidal category

symmetric monoidal category

\dagger
-compact closed category

\dagger
-compact closed category (
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(\mathbb{X})\simeq
CPM
(\mathbb{X})
)

Theorem
5.11
shows that the CP-infinity construction on any mixed unitary category produces an isomix category. Lemma
5.12
shows that if the base category has unitary duals, then the resulting category is dagger-isomix. Finally, it is shown in Lemma
5.13
that the CP-infinity construction is functorial in the presence of unitary duals.

Theorem 5.11
.

Given any mixed unitary categoy
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
,
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
is an isomix category.

Proof.

The units for
\widehat{\otimes}
and
\widehat{\oplus}
are
\top
and
\bot
respectively.

The linear distribution maps and all the basic basic natural isomorphisms are inherited from
\mathbb{X}
by composing each one of them with
(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}
i.e.,

\hfil A\widehat{\otimes}(B\widehat{\otimes}C)\xrightarrow{a_{\widehat{\otimes}}:=a_{\otimes}(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}}(A\widehat{\otimes}B)\widehat{\otimes}C\in\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})A\otimes(B\otimes C)\xrightarrow{a_{\otimes}}(A\otimes B)\otimes C\xrightarrow{(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}}\mathbb{C}\ /\sim

We prove that the associators and the other maps as defined above are natural isomorphisms in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
: From Lemma
5.10
,
Q:\mathbb{C}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
is functorial which means that all commuting diagrams and isomorphisms are preserved. It remains to show that Q preserves the linear structure and the mix map:

•

Q
preserves
\otimes
: Suppose
f:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A^{\prime}
and
g:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}
. Then,
Q(f)\widehat{\otimes}Q(g)=Q(f\otimes g)
:

\displaystyle Q(f)\widehat{\otimes}Q(g)

\displaystyle:=A\widehat{\otimes}B\xrightarrow{f(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}\widehat{\otimes}g(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}}(\bot\widehat{\oplus}\bot)\widehat{\oplus}(A^{\prime}\widehat{\otimes}B^{\prime})

\displaystyle Q(f\otimes g)

\displaystyle:=A\widehat{\otimes}B\xrightarrow{(f\otimes g)u_{\oplus}^{-1}}\bot\widehat{\oplus}(A^{\prime}\widehat{\otimes}B^{\prime})

Since,
\bot\oplus\bot\xrightarrow{u_{\oplus}^{L}}\bot
is a unitary isomorphism and,
f(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}\widehat{\otimes}g(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}(u_{\oplus}^{L}\oplus 1)=(f\otimes g)(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}\in\mathbb{C}
, by Lemma
5.4
,

f(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1})\widehat{\otimes}(g(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}\sim(f\otimes g)(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}

Therefore,
Q(f)\widehat{\otimes}Q(g)=Q(f\otimes g)
. Similarly,
Q(f)\widehat{\oplus}Q(g)=Q(f\oplus g)
.

•

Q
preserves all basic natural isomorphisms (associators, unitors, symmetry maps, mix map) and linear distributions:

To prove that
a_{\widehat{\otimes}}
is natural in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
, we need to prove that the following diagram commutes in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
:

\textstyle{A\widehat{\otimes}(B\widehat{\otimes}C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\widehat{\otimes}}}
\scriptstyle{(f\widehat{\otimes}g)\widehat{\otimes}h}
\textstyle{(A\widehat{\otimes}B)\widehat{\otimes}C\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{f\widehat{\otimes}(g\widehat{\otimes}h)}
\textstyle{A^{\prime}\widehat{\otimes}(B^{\prime}\widehat{\otimes}C^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{a_{\widehat{\otimes}}}
\textstyle{(A^{\prime}\widehat{\otimes}B^{\prime})\widehat{\otimes}C^{\prime}}

In other words, we need to show that the two compositions in
\mathbb{C}
are equivalent as Kraus maps. This is follows from Lemma
5.4
as there is a unitary isomorphism between the ancillary objects
\bot\oplus(U_{1}\oplus(U_{2}\oplus U_{3}))
and
\bot\oplus(U_{1}\oplus U_{2})\oplus U_{3}
. Similarly, we can show that the other basic linearly distrbutive transformations as defined are natural transformations. Since
Q
is functorial, it preserves isomorphisms and commuting diagrams so that the coherence diagrams automatically commute.

∎

The equality is proved by using the snake diagrams and
[U.2]
,
[U.5](b)
, and
[Udual.]
.

Suppose
f:A\rightarrow U_{1}\oplus B
and
g:B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U_{2}\oplus C
with
(\eta_{1},\varepsilon_{1}):U_{1}\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}V_{1}
and
(\eta_{2},\varepsilon_{2}):U_{2}\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}V_{2}
, then
\dagger
preserves composition, that is
(fg)^{\dagger}=g^{\dagger}f^{\dagger}
:

\hfil(fg)^{\dagger}:C^{\dagger}\rightarrow(V_{1}\otimes V_{2})^{\dagger}\oplus A^{\dagger}(fg):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(U_{1}\oplus U_{2})\oplus C

\hfil(g^{\dagger}f^{\dagger}):C^{\dagger}\rightarrow(V_{2}^{\dagger}\otimes V_{1}^{\dagger})\oplus A^{\dagger}g^{\dagger}:C^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U_{2}^{\dagger}\oplus B^{\dagger}~~~~~~~~~f^{\dagger}:B^{\dagger}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}U_{1}^{\dagger}\oplus A^{\dagger}

To prove that
(fg)^{\dagger}=(g^{\dagger}f^{\dagger})
in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
, represent the maps in circuit calculus and fuse the
\dagger
-boxes. Once the
\dagger
-boxes are fused, use
Lemma
5.4
to show that both Kraus operations belong to the same equivalence.
{\dagger}
preserves identity map since
((u_{\oplus}^{R})^{-1},u_{\oplus}^{L}):\top\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv_{~u}\bot
. Hence,
{\dagger}
is a functor.

All the basic natural isomorphisms associated with
\dagger
functor -
\lambda_{\oplus},\lambda_{\otimes},\lambda_{\bot},\lambda_{\top},\iota
- are lifted from
\mathbb{C}
using
Q:\mathbb{C}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
which is defined in Lemma
5.10
. The lifted morphisms are natural in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
since their ancillaries are unitarily isomorphic. Since
\dagger
is functorial, all commuting diagrams are preserved. By the same argument, unitary structure is preserved under
Q
.

Thus,
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
is a mixed unitary category: as
Q
preserves all unitary linear duals this makes
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
a
*
-MUdC.
∎

Lemma 5.13
.

The
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}
-construction is functorial on MUCs with unitary duals, that is,
*
-MUdCs.

Proof.

Let
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
and
M^{\prime}:\mathbb{U}^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}^{\prime}
be
*
-MUdCs and the following square be a MUC morphism:

\textstyle{\mathbb{U}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{M}
\scriptstyle{F_{u}}
\scriptstyle{\Downarrow~\alpha}
\textstyle{\mathbb{C}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F}
\textstyle{\mathbb{U}^{\prime}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{M^{\prime}}
\textstyle{\mathbb{C}^{\prime}}

F_{u}
and

are
\dagger
-isomix functors and

preserves unitary structure i.e.,

and (
n_{\bot}^{F_{u}}
or
m_{\top}^{F_{u}}
) is a unitary isomorphism.
\alpha
is a
\dagger
-linear natural isomorphism.

The natural isomorphism
\alpha
lifts to
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M^{\prime}:\mathbb{U}^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}^{\prime})
as follows:

\alpha^{\prime}:=[(\alpha_{u}(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}((n_{\bot}^{M^{\prime}})^{-1}\oplus 1),\bot)]:F(M(U))\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}M^{\prime}(F_{u}(U))

It is immediate that
\alpha^{\prime}_{U}:(G(Q(M(U_{1}):=F(M(U_{1})))\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(Q(M^{\prime}(F_{u}(U_{2}))):=M^{\prime}(F_{u}(U_{1}))
is an isomorphism. Let
U_{1}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to16.68407pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$f$}}}U_{2}\in\mathbb{U}
. To prove that
\alpha^{\prime}
is natural, we show that the following diagram commutes in
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M^{\prime}:\mathbb{U}^{\prime}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}^{\prime})
.

\textstyle{F(M(U_{1}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha^{\prime}_{U_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{[((F(M(f)(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}((n_{\bot}^{M})^{-1}\oplus 1))n_{\oplus}^{F}(\alpha\oplus 1)),F_{u}(\bot))]}
\textstyle{F(M(U_{2}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\alpha^{\prime}_{U_{2}}}
\textstyle{M^{\prime}(F_{u}(U_{1}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{[(M^{\prime}(F_{u}(f))(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}((n_{\bot}^{M^{\prime}})^{-1}\oplus 1),\bot)]}
\textstyle{M^{\prime}(F_{u}(U_{2}))}

The underlying Kraus maps for both the compositions are equivalent since
F_{u}(\bot)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to34.6118pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$(n_{\bot}^{F_{u}})^{-1}$}}}\bot
is unitarily isomorphic:

6
Environment structure for mixed unitary categories

In this section, we describe when a given isomix category is of form
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
for a MUC
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
by generalizing the notion of environment structures from
\dagger
-symmetric monoidal categories (see
[
13
]
) to mixed unitary categories. We then show that an environment structure over
M
which has purification is isomorphic to
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
.

An environment structure for a
\dagger
-symmetric monoidal category equips the category with the ability to discard any object in the category in a natural way, that is, there exists a natural transformation
\hbox to5.52pt{\vbox to7.23pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.76059pt\lower-2.76059pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 5.91 L 0 -1.18}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -3.54 -1.18 L 3.54 -1.18}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}

in the category. By generalizing the notion of environment structures to MUCs, one notices that it suffices to require discard maps only for the unitary objects
(A\simeq A^{\dagger})
and not for every object.

6.1
Environment structure and examples

The first task is to define environment structures and show that the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction gives an example of these structures.

Definition 6.2
.

An environment structure
F:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}
for a mixed unitary category
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
has
purification
if

•

F
is bijective on objects, and

•

for all
f:F(A)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F(B)\in\mathbb{D}
, there exists a Kraus map
(f^{\prime},U):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathbb{C}
such that

.

Moreover, this environment structure has purification.

Proof.

F
is functorial since
f(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}((n_{\bot}^{M})^{-1}\oplus 1)\sim f\sim(u_{\oplus}^{L})^{-1}(n_{\bot}^{M})^{-1}(1\oplus f)
. Define
F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}:=F
. Note that,
F
is a strict monoidal functor and an isomix functor.
In order to prove that
F:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}
with
satisfy axioms for environment structures, the properties of isomix functor and Lemma
5.4
are used.

To prove that this environment structure has purification, consider any map
[(f,U)]:A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
. Then, there exists a Kraus map
(f,U):A\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}B\in\mathbb{C}
. Then, the map in equation

6.2
Characterizing the
\mathsf{CP}
-infinity construction

In this section, we show that any environment structure with purification is initial in the category of environment structures. Given Lemma
6.3
, this shows that any environment structure over a
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
with purification is isomorphic to
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
Thus, environment structures with purification captures the abstract structure of
\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
.

Definition 6.4
.

Let
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
be a mixed unitary category. Define a category
\mathsf{Env}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
as follows:

Objects:

Environment structures for
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}

Arrows:

Suppose
D:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}
with
, and
D^{\prime}:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}^{\prime}
with
are two environment structures. Then, a morphism of environment structures is a strict isomix functor
F:\mathbb{D}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}^{\prime}
such that

•

\text{and, }F((u_{\otimes}^{L})_{A})=F((u_{\otimes}^{L})_{D(X)})=F(D((u_{\otimes}^{L})_{X}))=D^{\prime}((u_{\otimes}^{L})_{X})=(u_{\otimes}^{L})_{D^{\prime}(X)}=(u_{\otimes}^{L})_{F(D(X))}=(u_{\otimes}^{L})_{F(A)}

Smiliarly, it can be proved that
F
is strict comonoidal in
\oplus
.

Define
F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}:=F
and linear strengths to be identity maps. Thus,
F
is a unique strict Frobenius functor.
F
is an isomix functor because D and D’ preserve the mix map
{\sf m}
on the nose.
∎

Corollary 6.6
.

Suppose
D:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}
with
is an environment structure with purification for
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
. Then,
\mathbb{D}\simeq\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
.

Proof.

By Lemma
6.5
,
D:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{D}
with
is initial in
\mathsf{Env}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
. By Lemma
6.3
,
F:\mathbb{C}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
with
[(u_{\oplus}^{R})^{-1},U)]
is an environment structure for
M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C}
which has purification, hence it is also an initial object in
\mathsf{Env}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
. Since, initial objects of a category are isomorphic, there exists a strict isomix functor
\mathbb{D}\xrightarrow{F}\mathsf{CP}^{\infty}(M:\mathbb{U}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{C})
that is full and faithful.
∎

7
Summary

This article:

1.

describes a graphical calculus for mixed unitary categories,

2.

provides a description of completely positive maps in mixed unitary categories,

3.

generalizes the
CP
-infinity construction from dagger monoidal categories to the more general setting of mixed unitary categories, and

4.

characterizes the new
CP
-infinity construction for MUCs in terms of generalized environment structures.

Mixed unitary categories allow description of completely positive maps. Moreover, the richer type system of mixed unitary categories allows a larger collection of completely positive maps when compared to dagger monoidal categories. In particular, while all the completely positive maps must still factor through the self-adjoint core, positive maps can be between non-self-adjoint objects
(A\neq A^{\dagger})
.

The power of the type system of MUCs also becomes evident when characterizing the
CP
-infinity construction in terms of environment structures: in MUCs, one observes that discarding is available only for the self-adjoint (or unitary) objects.

The objective of developing mixed unitary categories is to show that they can be used as a semantics of higher-order quantum programming languages and protocols which employ infinite dimensional structures: the
CP
-infinity construction described in this article is a necessary step forward in this direction.

Appendix A
From Linearly distributive to monoidal categories

This section recalls the definition of mixed unitary categories introduced in
[
10
]
starting from linearly distributive categories
[
11
]
.

Linearly distributive categories (LDCs) are categories with two monoidal structures
(\otimes,\top,a_{\otimes},u_{\otimes}^{l},u_{\otimes}^{r})
and
(\oplus,\bot,a_{\oplus},u_{\oplus}^{l},u_{\oplus}^{r})
linked by natural transformations (which are not necessarily isomorphisms) called linear distributors:

\partial^{L}:A\otimes(B\oplus C)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}(A\otimes B)\oplus C~~~~~~~~~~~~~\partial^{R}:(A\oplus B)\otimes C\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}A\oplus(B\otimes C)

A monoidal category is an LDC in which both the monoidal structures coincide, and the right and the left distributor gives the associator and its inverse respectively. LDCs provide the categorical semantics for multiplicative linear logic without negation. Moreover, LDCs are equipped with graphical calculus that subsumes the graphical calculus of the monoidal categories
[
5
,
23
]
.

One shall ‘compact’ an LDC into a monoidal category in a series of steps as shown in Figure
3
. Along the way, one meets mix categories, isomix categories, and compact LDCs.

{\sf m}:\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\top
Isomix category
Compact LDC
A\otimes B\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to20.7889pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize$\mathsf{mx}$}}_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}A\oplus B
Monoidal category
\bot\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to18.25pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits^{\hbox{\scriptsize${\sf m}$}}_{\hbox{\scriptsize$\simeq$}}}\top

,

The natural transformation
\mathsf{mx}_{A,B}
is the
mixor
. When the map
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism, then the LDC is said to be an
isomix category
; furthermore,when
{\sf m}
is an isomorphism the coherence requirement above to obtain
{\sf mx}
is automatic (see Lemma 6.6
[
11
]
). A
compact LDC
is an isomix LDC in which the mixor is a natural isomorphism. For a
monoidal category
, the mixor is the identity natural transformation.

A.1
Linear duals

A key notion in the theory of LDCs is the notion of a linear dual.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
is a LDC and
A,B\in\mathbb{X}
, then
B
is
left linear dual
(or left linear adjoint) to
A
– or
A
is
right linear dual
(right linear adjoint) to
B
– written
(\eta,\varepsilon):B\dashv\!\!\!\!\dashv A
, if there exists
\eta:\top\rightarrow B\oplus A
and
\varepsilon:A\otimes B\rightarrow\bot
such that the following diagrams commute:

\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(u_{\otimes}^{L})^{-1}}
\textstyle{\top\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\eta\otimes 1}
\textstyle{(B\oplus A)\otimes B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial_{R}}
\textstyle{B}
\textstyle{B\oplus\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\oplus}^{R}}
\textstyle{B\oplus(A\otimes B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\oplus\varepsilon}

\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(u_{\otimes}^{R})^{-1}}
\textstyle{A\otimes\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{1\otimes\eta}
\textstyle{A\otimes(B\oplus A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\partial_{L}}
\textstyle{A}
\textstyle{\bot\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{u_{\oplus}^{L}}
\textstyle{(A\otimes B)\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\varepsilon\oplus 1}

An LDC in which every object has a chosen left and right dual is called a
*
-autonomous category
. In the above commuting diagrams, if
\mathbb{X}
is a monoidal category, then the distributor is replaced by the associator,
\partial^{R}=a_{\otimes}
and
\otimes=\oplus
. In such a case, one gets a compact closed category.

Appendix B
Linear functors and natural transformations

Having defined
\dagger
-isomix categories, we may now describe the appropirate functors between these categories. At a fundamental level, one would expect such functors to preserve the linear structure and the dagger. Functors between LDCs that preserve the linear structure are called linear functors. Given linearly distributive categories
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
, a linear functor
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
consists of

(i)

a pair of functors
F=(F_{\otimes},F_{\oplus})
:
F_{\otimes}
which is monoidal with respect to
\otimes
and
F_{\oplus}
which is comonoidal with respect to
\oplus

(ii)

natural transformations:

\displaystyle\nu_{\otimes}^{R}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A)\oplus F_{\otimes}(B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\otimes}^{L}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A\oplus B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\otimes}(A)\oplus F_{\oplus}(B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\oplus}^{R}

\displaystyle:F_{\otimes}(A)\otimes F_{\oplus}(B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A\otimes B)

\displaystyle\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

\displaystyle:F_{\oplus}(A)\otimes F_{\otimes}(B)\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}F_{\oplus}(A\otimes B)

such that the certain coherence conditions hold. See
[
12
, Definition 1]
for the complete definition.

Definition B.1
.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
are LDCs. A
Frobenius functor
is a linear functor
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
such that:

[FLF.1]

F_{\otimes}=F_{\oplus}

[FLF.2]

m_{\otimes}=\nu_{\oplus}^{R}=\nu_{\oplus}^{L}

[FLF.3]

n_{\oplus}=\nu_{\otimes}^{L}=\nu_{\otimes}^{R}

Observe that it follows by definition that for any
\dagger
-LDC
\mathbb{X}
,
(\_)^{\dagger}:\mathbb{X}^{\mathsf{op}}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{X}
is a Frobenius functor.

Definition B.2
.

Suppose
\mathbb{X}
and
\mathbb{Y}
are mix categories.
F:\mathbb{X}\allowbreak\mathrel{\mathop{\hbox to11.99998pt{\rightarrowfill}}\limits}\mathbb{Y}
is a
mix functor
if it is a Frobenius functor such that:

[mix-FF]

\textstyle{F(\bot)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{F({\sf m})}

\crvi

\crvi
\scriptstyle{n_{\bot}}
\textstyle{\bot\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{{\sf m}}
\textstyle{\top\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{m_{\top}}
\textstyle{F(\top)}

Lemma B.3
.

Mix functors preserve the mix map:

\textstyle{F(A)\otimes F(B)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\mathsf{mx}}
\scriptstyle{m_{\otimes}}
